newsitem.title: USA: UAW-Ford talks plod on, CEO hopeful for deal.
newsitem.headline: UAW-Ford talks plod on, CEO hopeful for deal.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. and the United Auto Workers union plodded on toward a new national labour contract Monday, and Ford Chairman Alex Trotman said he hoped a deal could be struck before the day's end.

Marathon bargaining sessions failed to produce an agreement covering the automaker's 105,000 UAW hourly workers, and bargainers resumed talks Monday after their first full night's sleep in about four days.

In a sign that talks may be nearing an end, a source close to the UAW confirmed that the union's executive board was scheduled to meet at 1 p.m. EDT Tuesday for a briefing on the progress of negotiations.
Any deal will need approval by the board, but the source said that was not necessarily the purpose of the meeting.

"I don't really know when they'll be finished. I hope they'll be finished today, but I don't know that," Trotman told reporters before a speech to the Economic Club of Detroit. Trotman was much more cautious than Ford Chief Financial Officer John Devine, who predicted to analysts last week that Ford would reach an agreement by Saturday.

He said the tone of the talks remained "positive and constructive," even though the automaker's plants on Tuesday had been operating for nearly two full days since Ford's past labour contract expired at midnight EDT Saturday.

There were few worries of a strike as production at Ford's U.S. assembly and components plants resumed on their normal schedules. Trotman said he did not expect the odds of a strike to increase as talks drag on past the deadline. The last national walkout over contract negotiations took place in 1976 against General Motors Corp..
"They've got to save their energy for GM," Bear Stearns & Co. auto analyst Nicholas Lobocarro said of the UAW. Analysts said talks with GM are expected to be more difficult than at Ford.
"There are a whole number of things still to be agreed on, but there's no dramatic single thing that is an issue of concern to the negotiating teams," Trotman said.
He said the automaker and the union have discussed several possible lengths for the contract beyond the typical three-year UAW pact, but declined to elaborate.
Ford has previously said that it would like an deal longer than the traditional three-year UAW contract because it would allow the automaker to stabilise its costs over a longer period.
UAW officials said in the morning that the two sides were close to an agreement, but were still at odds over the key issue of the use of outside suppliers, known as outsourcing.

In the pact affecting hourly workers, the union has sought to guarantee minimum employment levels and provisions that restrict the company's ability to shift work to outside suppliers, including establishing the right to strike over such decisions.

Also on the table was the length of time it takes for new workers to reach wage parity with veteran workers. In the previous pact, new hires started at 70 percent of the full, $19-an-hour wage, catching up to veteran workers after three years on the job.

Trotman added that the company needed to maintain a balance in the contract between meeting the union's needs and improving its own efficiency. "One of our key objectives as manufacturers is to maintain as much flexibility and competitiveness as we possibly can," he said.

Ford and the UAW on Sunday reached a tentative agreement covering about 750 salaried workers represented by the union, including designers and product development employees, according to union and company sources.
Trotman said Ford's bargaining teams were continuing to communicate with their counterparts at GM and Chrysler Corp., but he declined to say how a Ford-UAW agreement would affect those competitors.
The UAW traditionally uses the contract hammered out with the lead company as a pattern to be followed by the other two.
